Numbers 17:5: "Thus I will make to cease from me the grumblings of the people of Israel"
file_lines.text: The verse closes a long dispute over who God has chosen. It begins in Numbers 16. Korah and 250 chiefs, *"chosen from the assembly, well-known men"* (16:2; *qārîʾ*, H7148, "called"), rise up: *"Why then do you exalt yourselves above the assembly of the Lord?"* (16:3). Moses answers with God's choosing: *"The one whom he chooses he will bring near to him"* (16:5), and *"the man whom the Lord chooses shall be the holy one"* (16:7).

file_lines.section: Others around a choice, in the human inner being — the account from the §2c readings
file_lines.text: **Scope:** The account covers people who stand near a choice someone else made: at what was chosen, turned toward it, set against it, standing with the chosen, or knowing of the choice. In all but one of the readings the chooser is God. In 1Sa 20:30 it is Jonathan. God's own acts in reply (Num 17:5; Isa 45:4–5; 49:7; Jer 33:25–26; Rom 11:8; 1Pe 2:8) belong to 13.1 under rule 72. They are named here only where they answer what the others did. Readings beyond what a verse says are marked "I read".

file_lines.section: Set against the chosen
file_lines.text: **Grumbling, and seeking more.** When God's choice of Aaron was challenged, Moses named what lay under it: *"would you seek the priesthood also?"* (Num 16:10). The grumbling at Aaron was against God: *"What is Aaron that you grumble against him?"* (16:11), and God calls it *"the grumblings … which they grumble against you"*, to be made to *"cease from me"* (17:5). Psalm 106 names the inner act: *"men in the camp were jealous of Moses and Aaron"* (Psa 106:16). God's reply was to make the choice plain, with the staff that sprouted. Then the grumbling became terror: *"Are we all to perish?"* (Num 17:13).

verses.text: But you shall seek the place that the Lord your God will choose out of all your tribes to put his name and make his habitation there. There you shall go,

observations.text: Deut.12.5 'seek the place' draws on the 'resort to, frequent' sense (1a1) combined with devotional pursuit of the divinely chosen worship-site; a standard extension within the base gloss, no notable divergence.

In Deut.12.5, M15 (choose, of God choosing the place) is present but functions as God's own prior action, not something darash (Israel's seeking) directly modifies; the two characteristics operate on different agents (God chooses; the people seek) within the same verse without direct interaction.

What batch 1 adds
file_lines.text: - **The held phrasing in 10.7.** The working note in 10.7 holds the shared phrasing of Deuteronomy 23:16 (*"in the place that he shall choose within one of your towns, wherever it suits him"*) and Deuteronomy 12:5, 14. Batch 1 read Deuteronomy 12 in full. The forms of words differ: 12:5 has *"out of all your tribes"*, 12:14 *"in one of your tribes"*, and 23:16 *"within one of your towns"*. In 23:16 the chooser is the escaped slave. The reading does not settle whether the shared phrase is more than a form of words. It stays held.

file_lines.section: M64 "choose": batch 3 — choosing of one's own accord, choosing together, and the wisdom sayings
file_lines.text: - Deu 23:15–16, with Deu 12:5 and 12:14 for the phrase "the place that … shall choose"

file_lines.section: Deuteronomy 23:16 — "in the place that he shall choose … wherever it suits him"
file_lines.text: The phrase is a weighty one in Deuteronomy. *"the place that he shall choose within one of your towns"* has the same shape as the phrase Deuteronomy uses for the Lord’s own choosing: *"the place that the Lord your God will choose out of all your tribes"* (12:5); *"the place that the Lord will choose in one of your tribes"* (12:14). The words (place, that, choose, in one of your …) are the same (H4725, H0977). I read this as the law giving the escaped slave, in his own small measure, the kind of choosing the Lord keeps for his own dwelling. The verse does not draw the comparison.

file_lines.section: 8.3 The Ch 13 verses, by sub-chapter
The words
file_lines.text: The same verb is used of the Lord choosing the place for his name (Deu 12:5, 14), and of the Lord's answering choice: *"I also will choose harsh treatment for them"* (Isa 66:4).

file_lines.section: A choice that is honoured
file_lines.text: The phrase *"the place that he shall choose within one of your towns"* has the same wording as *"the place that the Lord your God will choose"* (Deu 12:5, 14). I read this as the law giving the slave a small share of the kind of choosing the Lord keeps for his own dwelling. The verse does not draw this comparison (open item).

file_lines.section: At the place God chose
file_lines.text: **Rejoicing.** *"And you shall rejoice before the Lord your God in all that you undertake"* (Deu 12:18). The joy is *"before the Lord"*, and its ground is given in the same chapter: *"in which the Lord your God has blessed you"* (12:7). At the Feast of Booths the joy is the purpose of the blessing: *"because the Lord your God will bless you … so that you will be altogether joyful"* (16:15). The place is where the joy is had. The blessing is what it is about.

Deuteronomy 18:6: "and he may come when he desires"
file_lines.text: "When he desires" is literally "with all the desire of his soul": *kol* (all; H3605) with *ʾawwāh* (desire; H0185) and *nepeš* (*soul: appetite*; H5315L). It is the same desire of the soul that is given room for meat in Deu 12:20–21. Here it is turned toward the chosen place.

file_lines.section: Desire, near and far
file_lines.text: - **Given room away from the place.** Ordinary meat need not be eaten at the chosen place. *"If the place that the Lord your God will choose to put his name there is too far from you, then you may kill … and you may eat within your towns whenever you desire"* (Deu 12:21). "Whenever you desire" is the soul's desire (*ʾawwāh*, desire, with *nepeš*, soul). It is spoken of plainly and allowed, with one limit: *"the blood is the life"* (12:23).

file_lines.section: At the place God chose
file_lines.text: **Learning to fear.** The tithe is eaten at the place *"that you may learn to fear the Lord your God always"* (14:23). The fear is learned at a meal. In the same passage the money is spent *"for whatever you desire … whatever your appetite craves. And you shall eat there before the Lord your God and rejoice"* (14:26). The passage does not set the fear, the appetite and the joy against each other.

file_lines.text: - It is learned at a feast in the chosen place (Deu 14:23).

file_lines.text: ## Deuteronomy 16:11 and 16:15: "you shall rejoice before the Lord your God" and "you will be altogether joyful"

file_lines.section: Deuteronomy 16:11 and 16:15: "you shall rejoice before the Lord your God" and "you will be altogether joyful"
file_lines.text: **The Feast of Weeks** is a feast of rejoicing: *"And you shall rejoice before the Lord your God, you and your son and your daughter, your male servant and your female servant, the Levite who is within your towns, the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow who are among you, at the place that the Lord your God will choose"* (v11). The next verse joins a remembering to it: *"You shall remember that you were a slave in Egypt; and you shall be careful to observe these statutes"* (v12). The list in v11 includes the servant and the sojourner. The verse after it reminds the one rejoicing that he was a slave.

file_lines.section: Deuteronomy 17:10: "And you shall be careful to do according to all that they direct you"
file_lines.text: - *"You shall not turn aside from the verdict that they declare to you, either to the right hand or to the left"* (v11).

file_lines.section: At the place God chose
file_lines.text: **Rejoicing.** *"And you shall rejoice before the Lord your God in all that you undertake"* (Deu 12:18). The joy is *"before the Lord"*, and its ground is given in the same chapter: *"in which the Lord your God has blessed you"* (12:7). At the Feast of Booths the joy is the purpose of the blessing: *"because the Lord your God will bless you … so that you will be altogether joyful"* (16:15). The place is where the joy is had. The blessing is what it is about.

file_lines.section: 8.3 The Ch 13 verses, by sub-chapter
At the place God chose
file_lines.text: **Carefulness, against presumption.** When a case is *"too difficult for you"* (17:8), the decision is sought at the place. What is asked of the person then is *"you shall be careful to do according to all that they direct you"* (17:10), and not to turn *"to the right hand or to the left"* (17:11). Presumption is the opposite, and the man who acts presumptuously dies. The end is that *"all the people shall hear and fear and not act presumptuously again"* (17:13). I read this as a person's own judgement reaching its limit and being asked to yield. The passage gives the limit (*"too difficult for you"*) and the carefulness. It does not describe the inner struggle.

file_lines.text: ### 6. Deu 23:16 — the escaped slave chooses where to live

file_lines.section: 6. Deu 23:16 — the escaped slave chooses where to live
file_lines.text: - **Choice:** the slave's: *"in the place that he shall choose within one of your towns, wherever it suits him"* (v16).

file_lines.section: 6. Deu 23:16 — the escaped slave chooses where to live
file_lines.text: - **Outcome:** Given as law, not narrated: *"He shall dwell with you, in your midst … You shall not wrong him"* (v16). Israel is to honour the choice and not hand him back: *"You shall not give up to his master"* (v15).

file_lines.section: What batch 1 adds
file_lines.text: - **The held phrasing in 10.7.** The working note in 10.7 holds the shared phrasing of Deuteronomy 23:16 (*"in the place that he shall choose within one of your towns, wherever it suits him"*) and Deuteronomy 12:5, 14. Batch 1 read Deuteronomy 12 in full. The forms of words differ: 12:5 has *"out of all your tribes"*, 12:14 *"in one of your tribes"*, and 23:16 *"within one of your towns"*. In 23:16 the chooser is the escaped slave. The reading does not settle whether the shared phrase is more than a form of words. It stays held.

file_lines.section: What batch 2 adds to the account of choosing
file_lines.text: **For the next batches:** batch 3 is people choosing of their own accord, and choosing together (Deu 23:16, 2Sa 19:38, 2Cor 8:17, Act 6:5, Act 15:22 and 25), with the wisdom sayings Pro 3:31 and 16:16. These are mostly not choices between God and other gods. Whether they show the same tie to what the eyes see, to delight and to knowing is to be read from them.

file_lines.section: Deuteronomy 23:16 — "in the place that he shall choose … wherever it suits him"
file_lines.text: ## Deuteronomy 23:16 — "in the place that he shall choose … wherever it suits him"

file_lines.section: Deuteronomy 23:16 — "in the place that he shall choose … wherever it suits him"
file_lines.text: The law concerns *"a slave who has escaped from his master to you"*. Israel is told *"You shall not give up to his master"* (v15). Then the choice is handed to the slave: *"He shall dwell with you, in your midst, in the place that he shall choose within one of your towns, wherever it suits him. You shall not wrong him"* (v16).

file_lines.section: What batch 3 adds to the account of choosing
file_lines.text: - **Choosing as a person's own freedom, honoured.** In Deu 23:16 and 2Sa 19:38 the ground is the chooser's own good: *"wherever it suits him"*, *"whatever seems good to you"*. Others are bound to honour it. This is a face not seen in batches 1–2, where the choosing was between the Lord and something else. Here "good in your eyes" is honoured. In Jos 24:15, "evil in your eyes" was where the choice against the Lord could start. The same expression changes character with the setting (#1919).

file_lines.section: What batch 3 adds to the account of choosing
file_lines.text: - Deu 23:16 echoes the phrase used for the place the Lord chooses (Deu 12). I have marked this "I read". Whether it is to be read as more than a shared form of words is for the researcher.

file_lines.section: Choosing in the human inner being — the account from the §2a readings
file_lines.text: - [batch 3](m64-choose-reading-batch3-own-accord-together-v1-20261007.md): Deu 23:16, 2Sa 19:38, 2Cor 8:17, Act 6:5, Act 15:22 and 25, Pro 3:31, Pro 16:16

file_lines.section: What choosing rests on
file_lines.text: **What is good to the chooser.** Two verses make the chooser's own good the ground, and honour it: *"wherever it suits him"* (Deu 23:16) and *"whatever seems good to you"* (2Sa 19:38). In Hebrew both say "the good" to him, or in his eyes.

file_lines.section: A choice that is honoured
file_lines.text: Choosing is a freedom a person can lose, and Scripture gives it back. The escaped slave *"shall dwell with you … in the place that he shall choose within one of your towns, wherever it suits him. You shall not wrong him"* (Deu 23:16). The king hands the choice to the man who fed him in the wilderness: *"all that you desire of me I will do for you"* (2Sa 19:38).

file_lines.section: What changes the character
file_lines.text: - **The choosing verb (H0977).** It is used for choosing a master (Jos 24:15), a place (Deu 23:16), a way (Psa 119:30; Isa 66:3), a preference (Pro 16:16), and a verdict (Job 34:4). *Why:* it is turned to whatever is set before a person.

file_lines.section: Still open
file_lines.text: - **Deu 23:16 and Deu 12.** Whether the shared phrase is more than a shared form of words (marked "I read").

file_lines.text: ### 1. Jos 24:15 — Israel at Shechem chooses whom to serve

file_lines.section: 1. Jos 24:15 — Israel at Shechem chooses whom to serve
file_lines.text: - **Led to:** Joshua recounts what the Lord gave: *"a land on which you had not labored"* (v13). Then he calls on them: *"fear the Lord and serve him in sincerity and in faithfulness. Put away the gods"* (v14). The choice is put to them on one condition: *"if it is evil in your eyes to serve the Lord, choose this day whom you will serve"* (v15).

file_lines.section: 1. Jos 24:15 — Israel at Shechem chooses whom to serve
file_lines.text: - Joshua chooses first: *"as for me and my house, we will serve the Lord"* (v15).

file_lines.section: 7. Judgement points for the researcher
file_lines.text: - Jos 24:15 and 22 (*"choose this day whom you will serve"*) make serving **what is chosen**. It is still counted as an operation.

file_lines.section: What batch 3 adds to the account of choosing
file_lines.text: - **Choosing as a person's own freedom, honoured.** In Deu 23:16 and 2Sa 19:38 the ground is the chooser's own good: *"wherever it suits him"*, *"whatever seems good to you"*. Others are bound to honour it. This is a face not seen in batches 1–2, where the choosing was between the Lord and something else. Here "good in your eyes" is honoured. In Jos 24:15, "evil in your eyes" was where the choice against the Lord could start. The same expression changes character with the setting (#1919).

file_lines.section: Whose measure
file_lines.text: - **The chooser's eyes.** *"if it is evil in your eyes to serve the Lord, choose this day"* (Jos 24:15). Here the chooser's own sight is where turning from the Lord could begin.

file_lines.section: What changes the character
file_lines.text: - It is the chooser's sight, from which turning from the Lord could begin (Jos 24:15).

file_lines.section: What changes the character
file_lines.text: - **The choosing verb (H0977).** It is used for choosing a master (Jos 24:15), a place (Deu 23:16), a way (Psa 119:30; Isa 66:3), a preference (Pro 16:16), and a verdict (Job 34:4). *Why:* it is turned to whatever is set before a person.

file_lines.section: Set against the chosen
file_lines.text: **Anger at what a choice costs.** Saul to Jonathan: *"do I not know that you have chosen the son of Jesse to your own shame"* (1Sa 20:30). Saul calls the choice shame and gives his reason: *"neither you nor your kingdom shall be established"* (20:31). His anger is for his house. It goes from insult to a death sentence to a spear thrown at his own son (20:33). Jonathan's choice was made in love, *"for he loved him as he loved his own soul"* (20:17). His own anger answers his father's, and it is grief for the one he chose: *"he was grieved for David, because his father had disgraced him"* (20:34). The choice holds, sealed by an oath *"in the name of the Lord"* (20:42).

observations.text: In 1 Sam 24.2 and 26.2, 'seek' carries a hostile-pursuit nuance (seeking to kill/capture David) rather than the neutral/benign 'seek to find' sense; this militarised sense diverges from the more affectionate or petitionary uses elsewhere (e.g. Song 3.1, Exod 10.11), showing the verb's flexibility to carry either amicable or adversarial intent depending on context.
Saul (party) initiates the seek-operation, directed toward David and his men (party), moving into the wilderness terrain to locate them -- a hostile pursuit operation.

M64 (chosen, of the men) is present but concerns selection/election rather than seeking; seeking here targets a person (David) not a quality, so no direct conceptual overlap with the co-present M-code.

file_lines.section: What the chosen are moved to
file_lines.text: - **Celebrating.** *"It was before the Lord, who chose me above your father and above all his house … and I will celebrate before the Lord"* (2Sa 6:21). The celebrating had stopped at Uzzah's death, when David was angry, afraid and unwilling (6:8–10). It came back when he heard of the Lord's blessing (6:12).

file_lines.section: Before whom
file_lines.text: The chosen live before God's sight, not others'. David answers Michal, who measured him by *"the eyes of his servants' female servants"* (2Sa 6:20): *"It was before the Lord, who chose me"*, and *"I will be abased in your eyes"* (6:21–22). The purpose of the choosing in Ephesians is to be holy and blameless *"before him"* (Eph 1:4).

file_lines.section: What batch 2 adds
file_lines.text: **Whose measure.** It comes up in four verses. Michal measures by *"the eyes of his servants' female servants"* (2Sa 6:20). The people in Jer 33:24 measure *"in their sight"*. Over against both, David celebrates *"before the Lord"* (2Sa 6:21), and Isa 49:7 gives the Lord's faithfulness and choosing. The same theme is in batch 1 (Deu 12:8) and in §2a ("whose measure").

Set against the chosen
file_lines.text: **Contempt in the heart.** Michal *"saw King David leaping and dancing before the Lord, and she despised him in her heart"* (2Sa 6:16). The contempt is inward before it is spoken. When it comes out, its measure is honour before others: *"before the eyes of his servants' female servants"* (6:20). David answers by naming the choosing: *"It was before the Lord, who chose me above your father"* (6:21).

file_lines.section: Set against the chosen
file_lines.text: **Whose eyes.** In four of these the measure is named, and it is set against God's: *"in his own eyes"* against the place God chooses (Deu 12:8); *"before the eyes of his servants' female servants"* against *"before the Lord"* (2Sa 6:20–21); *"in their sight"* (Jer 33:24); *"rejected by men but in the sight of God chosen"* (1Pe 2:4).

file_lines.text: ### 2. 2Sa 19:38 — Barzillai's choice for Chimham

file_lines.section: 2. 2Sa 19:38 — Barzillai's choice for Chimham
file_lines.text: - **Choice:** The king hands the choice to Barzillai: *"I will do for him whatever seems good to you, and all that you desire of me I will do for you"* (v38). The choice made is Barzillai's: Chimham goes in his place.

file_lines.section: What batch 2 adds to the account of choosing
file_lines.text: **For the next batches:** batch 3 is people choosing of their own accord, and choosing together (Deu 23:16, 2Sa 19:38, 2Cor 8:17, Act 6:5, Act 15:22 and 25), with the wisdom sayings Pro 3:31 and 16:16. These are mostly not choices between God and other gods. Whether they show the same tie to what the eyes see, to delight and to knowing is to be read from them.

file_lines.section: M64 "choose": batch 3 — choosing of one's own accord, choosing together, and the wisdom sayings
2 Samuel 19:38 — "whatever seems good to you, and all that you desire of me"
file_lines.text: ## 2 Samuel 19:38 — "whatever seems good to you, and all that you desire of me"

file_lines.section: What batch 3 adds to the account of choosing
file_lines.text: - **Choosing as a person's own freedom, honoured.** In Deu 23:16 and 2Sa 19:38 the ground is the chooser's own good: *"wherever it suits him"*, *"whatever seems good to you"*. Others are bound to honour it. This is a face not seen in batches 1–2, where the choosing was between the Lord and something else. Here "good in your eyes" is honoured. In Jos 24:15, "evil in your eyes" was where the choice against the Lord could start. The same expression changes character with the setting (#1919).

file_lines.section: 3.10 One's own decision, desire, accord (8)
file_lines.text: - "all that you desire of me I will do for you" (2Sa 19:38)

file_lines.section: Choosing in the human inner being — the account from the §2a readings
file_lines.text: - [batch 3](m64-choose-reading-batch3-own-accord-together-v1-20261007.md): Deu 23:16, 2Sa 19:38, 2Cor 8:17, Act 6:5, Act 15:22 and 25, Pro 3:31, Pro 16:16

file_lines.section: The words
file_lines.text: - *"desire"*: *"all that you desire of me I will do for you"* (2Sa 19:38)

file_lines.section: What choosing rests on
file_lines.text: **What is good to the chooser.** Two verses make the chooser's own good the ground, and honour it: *"wherever it suits him"* (Deu 23:16) and *"whatever seems good to you"* (2Sa 19:38). In Hebrew both say "the good" to him, or in his eyes.

file_lines.section: Whose measure
file_lines.text: Yet "good in your eyes" is not always the wrong measure. When the king says *"whatever seems good to you"* to the old man who served him (2Sa 19:38), the chooser's own eyes are honoured. The setting changes what the same expression means. (See "What changes the character" below.)

file_lines.section: A choice that is honoured
file_lines.text: Choosing is a freedom a person can lose, and Scripture gives it back. The escaped slave *"shall dwell with you … in the place that he shall choose within one of your towns, wherever it suits him. You shall not wrong him"* (Deu 23:16). The king hands the choice to the man who fed him in the wilderness: *"all that you desire of me I will do for you"* (2Sa 19:38).

file_lines.section: What changes the character
file_lines.text: - It is the chooser's own good, honoured by the king (2Sa 19:38).

file_lines.section: Turned toward it from far off
file_lines.text: Nehemiah prays from exile in the same verb. He asks God to remember his word to Moses: *"if you return to me and keep my commandments and do them, … from there I will gather them and bring them to the place that I have chosen"* (Neh 1:9). Here the return is to God himself, and the place is where he brings those who return. Nehemiah's own part comes first: he *"sat down and wept and mourned for days"* (1:4), and confessed *"Even I and my father's house have sinned"* (1:6).

file_lines.section: 1. Wanting life itself, and wanting to "see good"
file_lines.text: **What lies behind it: the same phrase, lost.** Job uses the same words for the opposite state: *"Remember that my life is a breath; my eye will never again see good"* (Job 7:7, in Ch 2). The psalm's "desires life … that he may see good" and Job's "never again see good" are one phrase. **I read** that the want for life is a want to see good. Where the hope of seeing good is gone, life itself is weighed as a breath, and then loathed (Job 7:15–16, in Ch 2). The verses do not say this is a sequence. They use the one phrase for both states.

file_lines.text: > **Q1 citation: ❗ Needs attention.** Ch 2 *Wanting to die* is accurate. No one weighs this choice: it is Job's own would-be choice, spoken to God in complaint. It belongs with the next bullet, *Choosing between death and life*. This is a working note, not narrative text.

file_lines.section: Job 7:15: "so that I would choose strangling and death rather than my bones"
file_lines.text: Job speaks *"in the anguish of my spirit … in the bitterness of my soul"* (v11). The choice follows from what is done to him at night: *"When I say, 'My bed will comfort me' … then you scare me with dreams and terrify me with visions, so that I would choose strangling and death"* (vv13–15). He goes on: *"I loathe my life; I would not live forever. Leave me alone"* (v16).

file_lines.text: His evaluation: *"Take care; do not turn to iniquity, for this you have chosen rather than affliction"* (v21). The choice he sees is a preference, as in Proverbs 16:16 (*"rather than"*). Of the two things before Job, affliction (H6040, the word in v15) and iniquity (H0205), Elihu says Job has taken iniquity rather than accept the affliction as the opening of his ear. The warning *"Take care"* treats the choice as still able to be turned.

file_lines.text: - The person's fear: *"Who is the man who fears the Lord? Him will he instruct in the way that he should choose"* (v12).

file_lines.section: What batch 1 adds
file_lines.text: **Being chosen comes before the inner act, not after it.** In §2a, knowing, fear and teaching came before a person's own choosing (Isa 7:15; Psa 25:12). In Isaiah 43:10, God chooses first, and knowing is the purpose. The chosen were blind and deaf when chosen (43:8). In Psalm 65 they were chosen after their iniquity was atoned for (v3–4).

Psalm 25:12 — "Him will he instruct in the way that he should choose"
file_lines.text: ## Psalm 25:12 — "Him will he instruct in the way that he should choose"

file_lines.section: Psalm 25:12 — "Him will he instruct in the way that he should choose"
file_lines.text: Then comes the verse: *"Who is the man who fears the Lord? Him will he instruct in the way that he should choose"* (v12). The word "instruct" is the same in v8 and v12 (H3384B). The person who chooses here does not make up the way. The way to choose is taught, and the one who is taught it is the one who fears the Lord. The fear comes first, then the teaching, then the choice. The verse does not say the man chooses well on his own; it says the Lord instructs him in what he should choose.

file_lines.section: What batch 2 adds to the account of choosing
file_lines.text: - **The way to choose is taught (Psa 25:8, 12).** The Lord instructs sinners and the humble out of his goodness, and the one who fears him is taught *"the way that he should choose"*. This stands beside Psalm 119:29, where the psalmist asks God to put the false way far off. In both psalms the chooser does not stand alone.

file_lines.section: What batch 2 adds to the account of choosing
file_lines.text: - **Fear of the Lord comes before the choosing (Psa 25:12, 14).** The test reading of Joshua 24 had *"fear the Lord and serve him"* (v14) before the choice. Psalm 25 puts the fear first explicitly: it is the man who fears whom the Lord instructs.

file_lines.section: Job 36:21 — Elihu: "this you have chosen rather than affliction"
file_lines.text: He ends by pointing to God: *"who is a teacher like him?"* (v22). "Teacher" here is H4175, from the same root as *"instruct"* in Psalm 25:8, 12 (H3384).

file_lines.section: What choosing rests on
file_lines.text: **Being taught.** *"Who is the man who fears the Lord? Him will he instruct in the way that he should choose"* (Psa 25:12). The teaching comes from who the Lord is: *"Good and upright is the Lord; therefore he instructs sinners in the way"* (25:8). The psalmist asks for it: *"Make me to know your ways, O Lord; teach me your paths"* (25:4). In Psalm 119 he asks *"graciously teach me your law"*, and asks God to do the refusing with him: *"Put false ways far from me"* (119:29).

file_lines.section: What choosing rests on
file_lines.text: **The fear of the Lord.** In Psalm 25 the fear comes first, then the teaching, then the choice (25:12). Joshua puts the same order before the people: *"fear the Lord and serve him in sincerity and in faithfulness"* (Jos 24:14), and then *"choose this day"*.

file_lines.section: What batch 1 adds
file_lines.text: In 2Sa 6:21, 1Ch 28:10, Isa 43:10 and Isa 44:2 the verse names the being chosen as the ground or the reason. In Psa 65:4 the response follows the choosing in the same sentence. In Psa 105:43 and 106:5, "chosen ones" names the people whose joy it is; the verse does not make the choosing the cause.

file_lines.section: What batch 1 adds
file_lines.text: **Being chosen comes before the inner act, not after it.** In §2a, knowing, fear and teaching came before a person's own choosing (Isa 7:15; Psa 25:12). In Isaiah 43:10, God chooses first, and knowing is the purpose. The chosen were blind and deaf when chosen (43:8). In Psalm 65 they were chosen after their iniquity was atoned for (v3–4).

file_lines.section: Psalm 105:43: "his chosen ones with singing"
file_lines.text: The verse follows straight on: *"So he brought his people out with joy, his chosen ones with singing"* (v43). The joy and singing are set on the people brought out. They come with being brought out, and the bringing out comes from God remembering his promise. The chosen are told to remember (v5) because he remembered (v8, v42).

file_lines.section: What batch 1 adds
file_lines.text: In 2Sa 6:21, 1Ch 28:10, Isa 43:10 and Isa 44:2 the verse names the being chosen as the ground or the reason. In Psa 65:4 the response follows the choosing in the same sentence. In Psa 105:43 and 106:5, "chosen ones" names the people whose joy it is; the verse does not make the choosing the cause.

file_lines.section: What batch 1 adds
file_lines.text: **The return is the Lord's remembering.** He remembered his covenant at their cry (Psa 106:44–45). He remembered his promise and brought them out with joy (Psa 105:42–43). He blots out their sins and will not remember them (Isa 43:25). The chosen are called to remember in turn (Psa 105:5; Isa 44:21).

verses.text: Therefore he said he would destroy them— had not Moses, his chosen one, stood in the breach before him, to turn away his wrath from destroying them.

observations.text: Intercession: standing in the breach; driven by the intercessor's own fear; answered (Moses), forbidden (Jer 7:16), sought and not found (Eze 22:30), refused (Eze 9:8), insufficient (Eze 14:20), turned to imprecation (Jer 18:20–23); and the one explained by God's anger prays for the explainers (Job 42:8)
Moses names his own fear of the wrath (Deu 9:19). Ezekiel's cry is a question. Jeremiah recalls his past intercession, then asks for the wrath. AG-33, AN-55.

file_lines.section: With the chosen, and for them
file_lines.text: The chosen also stand for the others. *"Therefore he said he would destroy them—had not Moses, his chosen one, stood in the breach before him, to turn away his wrath"* (Psa 106:23). The psalm calls Moses chosen at the moment he stands for people who *"forgot God"* (106:21). The same psalm says those people were jealous of him (106:16), and that later *"they made his spirit bitter, and he spoke rashly with his lips"* (106:33). The psalm sets these side by side and does not comment.

file_lines.text: ## Psalm 119:30 — "I have chosen the way of faithfulness"

file_lines.section: Psalm 119:30 — "I have chosen the way of faithfulness"
file_lines.text: The false way is not refused by his own strength alone. He asks God to put it at a distance. Then he states the choice: *"I have chosen the way of faithfulness; I set your rules before me"* (v30). The choosing is joined at once to keeping something in view: he puts the rules in front of himself, where he can see them.

file_lines.section: Choosing in the human inner being — the account from the §2a readings
file_lines.text: - [the test](m64-choose-test-reading-v1-20261007.md): Jos 24:15, Psa 119:30, Isa 65:12

file_lines.section: Making the choice, and holding it
file_lines.text: - **It is held by keeping in view and clinging.** *"I have chosen the way of faithfulness; I set your rules before me. I cling to your testimonies"* (Psa 119:30–31). The verb for "cling" is the one used two verses earlier: *"My soul clings to the dust"* (119:25). What the soul clings to has turned.

file_lines.section: What changes the character
file_lines.text: - **The choosing verb (H0977).** It is used for choosing a master (Jos 24:15), a place (Deu 23:16), a way (Psa 119:30; Isa 66:3), a preference (Pro 16:16), and a verdict (Job 34:4). *Why:* it is turned to whatever is set before a person.

file_lines.text: - *"Because they hated knowledge and did not choose the fear of the Lord, would have none of my counsel and despised all my reproof, therefore they shall eat the fruit of their way, and have their fill of their own devices"* (Pro 1:29–31).

file_lines.section: 1.3 Refusing God: what was offered, and what it was refused for
file_lines.text: **Pro 1:29–31 and Psa 81:11–12 put choosing, willing and one's own counsels or devices into a single sentence.** In Proverbs: did not choose, would have none of my counsel, their own devices. In the psalm: would not submit, their stubborn hearts, their own counsels. These are the places where Scripture itself sets the acts side by side. Both say what follows: being given over to one's own counsels, and being filled with one's own devices. They do not say these acts form one sequence in every person, and these notes do not say it either.

file_lines.section: 2.2 Passages where Scripture itself puts them together
file_lines.text: 1. **Pro 1:29–31.** Did not choose the fear of the Lord, would have none of my counsel, are filled with their own devices: choosing, willing and devising in one sentence. Earlier in the same chapter, *"if sinners entice you, do not consent. If they say, 'Come with us, let us lie in wait for blood'"* (1:10–11) puts the will's "no" right against a group plot. That is plotting as written in 10.10.

file_lines.section: Choosing in the human inner being — the account from the §2a readings
file_lines.text: Scripture does not stop to define choosing. In these verses it shows choosing as an act with two sides. The clearest sentence is about a child: *"when he knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good"* (Isa 7:15). Refusing and choosing are one act, seen from either side. The man the book of Job calls blameless is described by his refusing: he *"feared God and turned away from evil"* (Job 1:1). The father in Proverbs puts the choice entirely in the negative: *"do not choose any of his ways"* (Pro 3:31).

file_lines.section: What draws it
file_lines.text: **Envy.** The pull can be named before the choice, and the command reaches it: *"Do not envy a man of violence and do not choose any of his ways"* (Pro 3:31).

file_lines.section: Proverbs 16:16 — "To get understanding is to be chosen rather than silver"
file_lines.text: ## Proverbs 16:16 — "To get understanding is to be chosen rather than silver"

file_lines.section: What batch 3 adds to the account of choosing
file_lines.text: - **Choosing as preferring.** *"to be chosen rather than silver"* (Pro 16:16): to choose is to weigh and set above. What is to be preferred is inward, and it is valued above *"nothing you desire"* (Pro 3:15).

file_lines.section: Job 36:21 — Elihu: "this you have chosen rather than affliction"
file_lines.text: His evaluation: *"Take care; do not turn to iniquity, for this you have chosen rather than affliction"* (v21). The choice he sees is a preference, as in Proverbs 16:16 (*"rather than"*). Of the two things before Job, affliction (H6040, the word in v15) and iniquity (H0205), Elihu says Job has taken iniquity rather than accept the affliction as the opening of his ear. The warning *"Take care"* treats the choice as still able to be turned.

file_lines.section: The words
file_lines.text: - *"to be chosen"* in the sense of preferred: *"To get understanding is to be chosen rather than silver"* (Pro 16:16)

file_lines.section: What draws it
file_lines.text: **Preferring.** To choose can be to weigh one good against another and set it above: *"How much better to get wisdom than gold! To get understanding is to be chosen rather than silver"* (Pro 16:16). Proverbs 3 sets the weighing against all desire: *"nothing you desire can compare with her"* (3:15).

file_lines.section: What changes the character
file_lines.text: - **The choosing verb (H0977).** It is used for choosing a master (Jos 24:15), a place (Deu 23:16), a way (Psa 119:30; Isa 66:3), a preference (Pro 16:16), and a verdict (Job 34:4). *Why:* it is turned to whatever is set before a person.

file_lines.text: ### 20. Isa 7:15–16 — the child who knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good

file_lines.section: F. Points for the researcher
file_lines.text: - **F3. Isa 7:15–16 (entry 20).** The verses name a capacity to choose, not a choice made. It stays in §2a as "ground", but it is a different kind of entry from the others.

file_lines.section: Psalm 106:5: "that I may rejoice in the gladness of your nation"
file_lines.text: "Despised" in v24 is H3988A, the same word as *"refuse the evil"* in Isaiah 7:15. The chosen people refused what they were given. "Faith" in v24 is H0539, the same word as *"believed"* in v12. The psalm has them believing, then forgetting, then without faith.

file_lines.section: Isaiah 43:10: "my servant whom I have chosen, that you may know and believe me and understand"
file_lines.text: This is the reverse of the order in §2a, where the child chooses *"when he knows how"* (Isa 7:15). There the knowing comes before the person's own choosing. Here, the knowing follows God's choosing of the person. Each verse states its own order.

file_lines.section: What batch 1 adds
file_lines.text: **Being chosen comes before the inner act, not after it.** In §2a, knowing, fear and teaching came before a person's own choosing (Isa 7:15; Psa 25:12). In Isaiah 43:10, God chooses first, and knowing is the purpose. The chosen were blind and deaf when chosen (43:8). In Psalm 65 they were chosen after their iniquity was atoned for (v3–4).

Jeremiah 33:24: "'The Lord has rejected the two clans that he chose'? Thus they have despised my people"
file_lines.text: Others look at the state of the chosen and draw a conclusion about God: he has rejected them. Their contempt rests on that conclusion. "Despised" is *nāʾaṣ* (*to spurn*; H5006). The measure is their own: *"in their sight"*. "Rejected" is *māʾas* (H3988A), the same verb as *"refuse the evil"* in Isaiah 7:15 (§2a).

file_lines.text: ## Isaiah 7:15–16 — "when he knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good"

file_lines.section: Isaiah 7:15–16 — "when he knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good"
file_lines.text: The sign is given anyway, and at its centre is a child who has what Ahaz lacked: *"He shall eat curds and honey when he knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good"* (v15). The act is one act with two sides:

file_lines.section: What batch 1 adds to the account of choosing
file_lines.text: - **Refusing is choosing (Isa 7:15–16).** The act is one act with two sides, and refusing can go either way. The child refuses the evil. Ahaz refuses the sign, and the people refuse the gentle waters (8:6), with the same verb. This sharpens the test reading of Isa 65:12, which said that not answering and not listening are already choosing: in Isa 8:6 the refusal is named outright.

file_lines.section: What batch 1 adds to the account of choosing
file_lines.text: - **Choosing rests on knowing how (Isa 7:15).** It is a knowing *how* to tell evil from good and turn. In Isa 1 the oracle opens with its absence: *"Israel does not know, my people do not understand"* (1:3).

file_lines.section: What batch 1 adds to the account of choosing
file_lines.text: - **The choice is laid out as an offer, with both outcomes (Isa 1:16–20).** *"cease to do evil, learn to do good"*; *"willing"* or *"refuse"*; eat, or be eaten. In Isa 7:15 the right choice also ends in eating.

file_lines.section: Psalm 25:12 — "Him will he instruct in the way that he should choose"
file_lines.text: - *"His soul shall abide in well-being, and his offspring shall inherit the land"* (v13). "Well-being" here (H2896B) is the same word as *"the good"* in Isaiah 7:15, *"refuse the evil and choose the good"*. The man taught the way he should choose has his soul *"abide"*, lodge or stay, in the good.

file_lines.section: Psalm 25:12 — "Him will he instruct in the way that he should choose"
file_lines.text: The psalmist then turns his eyes: *"My eyes are ever toward the Lord, for he will pluck my feet out of the net"* (v15). Where the eyes are turned decides where the feet are kept from.

file_lines.section: What batch 2 adds to the account of choosing
file_lines.text: - **The good chosen is the good the soul lives in.** Isaiah 7:15 has *"choose the good"*, and Psalm 25:13 has *"His soul shall abide in well-being"*. It is the same word (H2896B). I read this as the good that is chosen becoming the place where the soul lives. Each verse says its own half; neither refers to the other.

file_lines.section: 2 Samuel 19:38 — "whatever seems good to you, and all that you desire of me"
file_lines.text: Barzillai declines, and his reason is about his own inner capacity: *"I am this day eighty years old. Can I discern what is pleasant and what is not? Can your servant taste what he eats or what he drinks? Can I still listen to the voice of singing men and singing women?"* (v35). The Hebrew is "know between good and evil" (H3045 with H0996, H2896B, H7451A). It is the same pairing as Isaiah 7:15–16, *"knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good"*. Here it is the knowing of taste and pleasure, and Barzillai says that at eighty it has gone. The same words, put to the palate rather than to right and wrong, mark a change of face (#1919).

file_lines.section: What batch 3 adds to the account of choosing
file_lines.text: - **The knowing of good and evil has more than one face.** In Isa 7:15 it is the knowing that grounds choosing the good. In 2Sa 19:35 the same words are the palate's knowing of pleasant and unpleasant, and they fade with age.

file_lines.section: Job 34:33 — Elihu: "For you must choose, and not I"
file_lines.text: - **The refusing word comes back.** *"because you reject it"* uses H3988A, the same verb as *"refuse the evil"* in Isaiah 7:15. Elihu says Job is refusing, and that God will not repay on Job's terms because of it.

file_lines.section: What batch 4 adds to the account of choosing
file_lines.text: - **The refusing verb returns at the end.** Elihu's *"you reject"* and Job's *"I despise … and repent"* are the same verb (34:33; 42:6), the verb of *"refuse the evil"* (Isa 7:15). In Job the choice is made when *"now my eye sees you"* (42:5). This stands beside the test reading of Jos 24, where the people chose from what they had seen.

file_lines.section: Choosing in the human inner being — the account from the §2a readings
file_lines.text: Scripture does not stop to define choosing. In these verses it shows choosing as an act with two sides. The clearest sentence is about a child: *"when he knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good"* (Isa 7:15). Refusing and choosing are one act, seen from either side. The man the book of Job calls blameless is described by his refusing: he *"feared God and turned away from evil"* (Job 1:1). The father in Proverbs puts the choice entirely in the negative: *"do not choose any of his ways"* (Pro 3:31).

file_lines.section: The words
file_lines.text: - *"refuse the evil"* (Isa 7:15)

file_lines.section: Choosing has two sides
file_lines.text: Refusing is itself choosing. The child *"knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good"* (Isa 7:15). The oracle around that verse shows refusing going both ways. Ahaz refuses the Lord's offer of a sign with pious words: *"I will not ask, and I will not put the Lord to the test"* (Isa 7:12). The people *"refused the waters of Shiloah that flow gently"* (8:6). The right refusing and the wrong refusing are set in one oracle, each with its own consequence.

file_lines.section: What choosing rests on
file_lines.text: **Knowing how.** The child chooses *"when he knows how"* (Isa 7:15). The oracle of Isaiah 1 opens with the absence of that knowing: *"Israel does not know, my people do not understand"* (1:3).

file_lines.section: What follows the choice
file_lines.text: - *"His soul shall abide in well-being"* (Psa 25:13). "Well-being" is the same word as *"the good"* in *"choose the good"* (Isa 7:15). I read this as the good that is chosen becoming the place the soul lives.

file_lines.section: What follows the choice
file_lines.text: - The child who refuses the evil and chooses the good eats *"curds and honey"*, the food of *"everyone who is left in the land"* (Isa 7:15, 22). In the other oracle, *"If you are willing and obedient, you shall eat the good of the land"* (Isa 1:19).

file_lines.section: What changes the character
file_lines.text: - It is the knowing that grounds the moral choice (Isa 7:15–16).

file_lines.section: What changes the character
file_lines.text: - It is refusing the evil (Isa 7:15).

file_lines.text: ## Isaiah 7:15–16 — "when he knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good"

file_lines.section: Isaiah 7:15–16 — "when he knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good"
file_lines.text: The next verse sets a second consequence against the same knowing: *"before the boy knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good, the land whose two kings you dread will be deserted"* (v16). What Ahaz feared will be gone. Then comes what Ahaz’s own choice brings on him: *"The Lord will bring upon you and upon your people and upon your father’s house such days as have not come … the king of Assyria!"* (v17).

file_lines.section: What batch 1 adds to the account of choosing
file_lines.text: - **Refusing is choosing (Isa 7:15–16).** The act is one act with two sides, and refusing can go either way. The child refuses the evil. Ahaz refuses the sign, and the people refuse the gentle waters (8:6), with the same verb. This sharpens the test reading of Isa 65:12, which said that not answering and not listening are already choosing: in Isa 8:6 the refusal is named outright.

file_lines.section: 2 Samuel 19:38 — "whatever seems good to you, and all that you desire of me"
file_lines.text: Barzillai declines, and his reason is about his own inner capacity: *"I am this day eighty years old. Can I discern what is pleasant and what is not? Can your servant taste what he eats or what he drinks? Can I still listen to the voice of singing men and singing women?"* (v35). The Hebrew is "know between good and evil" (H3045 with H0996, H2896B, H7451A). It is the same pairing as Isaiah 7:15–16, *"knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good"*. Here it is the knowing of taste and pleasure, and Barzillai says that at eighty it has gone. The same words, put to the palate rather than to right and wrong, mark a change of face (#1919).

verses.text: He who is too impoverished for an offering chooses wood that will not rot; he seeks out a skillful craftsman to set up an idol that will not move.

observations.text: In Isa 40.20 'seeks out' functions within the base gloss of seeking-to-secure (a craftsman), a straightforward practical-search sense with no notable added nuance.
The impoverished man (implied party, 'he') initiates the seeking-operation, directed toward a skillful craftsman (party) to make an idol -- seeking here serves an idolatrous construction project.

M64 (chooses, wood-selection), M16 (skillful), M23/M55 (setting up an idol) are present but describe separate stages of idol-making; seeking here specifically targets the craftsman, distinct from those other characteristics' own referents.

file_lines.section: What batch 1 adds
file_lines.text: In 2Sa 6:21, 1Ch 28:10, Isa 43:10 and Isa 44:2 the verse names the being chosen as the ground or the reason. In Psa 65:4 the response follows the choosing in the same sentence. In Psa 105:43 and 106:5, "chosen ones" names the people whose joy it is; the verse does not make the choosing the cause.

file_lines.section: What batch 1 adds
file_lines.text: **Being chosen comes before the inner act, not after it.** In §2a, knowing, fear and teaching came before a person's own choosing (Isa 7:15; Psa 25:12). In Isaiah 43:10, God chooses first, and knowing is the purpose. The chosen were blind and deaf when chosen (43:8). In Psalm 65 they were chosen after their iniquity was atoned for (v3–4).

file_lines.section: What batch 1 adds
file_lines.text: **For batch 2:** the 8 New Testament verses. In five of them (Eph 1:4, 2Th 2:13, Tit 1:1, Jam 2:5, 2Pe 1:10) the inner act is given as the purpose of the choosing, or as the call that follows it. Whether they keep the order seen in Isaiah 43:10, with the choosing first and the knowing after, is to be read from them.

file_lines.section: 1 Chronicles 28:10: "the Lord has chosen you … be strong and do it"
file_lines.text: David speaks to the whole assembly, then to Solomon. He begins with his own heart and its refusal: *"I had it in my heart to build a house of rest for the ark"* (v2), *"But God said to me, 'You may not build a house for my name'"* (v3). The man who says *"the Lord God of Israel chose me"* (v4) was refused what was in his heart. Being chosen did not give David everything he intended.

He made, he formed, he will help, and he has chosen. The chosen person is not told to be brave. He is told who has chosen him.

file_lines.section: Others around a choice, in the human inner being — the account from the §2c readings
file_lines.text: **Scope:** The account covers people who stand near a choice someone else made: at what was chosen, turned toward it, set against it, standing with the chosen, or knowing of the choice. In all but one of the readings the chooser is God. In 1Sa 20:30 it is Jonathan. God's own acts in reply (Num 17:5; Isa 45:4–5; 49:7; Jer 33:25–26; Rom 11:8; 1Pe 2:8) belong to 13.1 under rule 72. They are named here only where they answer what the others did. Readings beyond what a verse says are marked "I read".

file_lines.section: Knowing that a choice was made, and not knowing
file_lines.text: **Not knowing, and still used.** Cyrus is called for the sake of the chosen: *"For the sake of my servant Jacob, and Israel my chosen, I call you by your name, I name you, though you do not know me"* (Isa 45:4). And *"I equip you, though you do not know me"* (45:5). Knowing is held out as the purpose: *"that you may know that it is I"* (45:3).

file_lines.section: What changes the character (#1919)
file_lines.text: - Not knowing God does not stop a man from being called for the sake of the chosen (Isa 45:4–5).

file_lines.section: What batch 2 adds
file_lines.text: **Whose measure.** It comes up in four verses. Michal measures by *"the eyes of his servants' female servants"* (2Sa 6:20). The people in Jer 33:24 measure *"in their sight"*. Over against both, David celebrates *"before the Lord"* (2Sa 6:21), and Isa 49:7 gives the Lord's faithfulness and choosing. The same theme is in batch 1 (Deu 12:8) and in §2a ("whose measure").

file_lines.section: What batch 2 adds
file_lines.text: **What God does in reply.** In Num 17:5 he makes the choice plain. In Isa 49:7 he promises that kings will bow. In Jer 33:25–26 he points to the fixed order of day and night. Under rule 72 these acts are God's and go to Ch 13. They are recorded here because each one answers what the others did.

file_lines.section: What batch 2 adds
file_lines.text: **The same word in two verses.** Michal's *"despised"* (2Sa 6:16) and the servant *"deeply despised"* (Isa 49:7) are the same verb, *bāzâ* (H0959). The verses are side by side. The text does not join them.

file_lines.section: Isaiah 56:4 — "who choose the things that please me and hold fast my covenant"
file_lines.text: ## Isaiah 56:4 — "who choose the things that please me and hold fast my covenant"

file_lines.section: Isaiah 56:4 — "who choose the things that please me and hold fast my covenant"
file_lines.text: Then he describes the eunuchs he means: *"who keep my Sabbaths, who choose the things that please me and hold fast my covenant"* (v4). The word "please" is H2654A, the same word as *"delight"* in Isaiah 65:12 and 66:4 (*"chose what I did not delight in"*, *"chose that in which I did not delight"*). Here the choosing goes the other way. These choose what the Lord delights in. The measure is the same as in those two oracles, the Lord's delight, and here it is met.

file_lines.section: What batch 2 adds to the account of choosing
file_lines.text: - **Choosing what the Lord delights in (Isa 56:4).** This is the counterpart to Isaiah 65:12 and 66:4. With the three verses together, "the things that please me" and "what I did not delight in" are the two sides of one measure.

file_lines.section: What batch 2 adds to the account of choosing
file_lines.text: - **The choice is held, not just made.** It is set between keeping and holding fast (Isa 56:2, 4, 6), and between eyes turned to the Lord and waiting (Psa 25:15, 21). This sits with the test readings: the heart inclined after the choice (Jos 24:23), and clinging to the testimonies (Psa 119:31).

file_lines.section: An inner act weighed by what God chooses
file_lines.text: In one passage the inner act of the others is itself set against God's choosing. The people fast and ask, *"Why have we humbled ourselves, and you take no knowledge of it?"* (Isa 58:3). They *"delight to know my ways"* and *"delight to draw near to God"* (58:2). Yet *"in the day of your fast you seek your own pleasure, and oppress all your workers"* (58:3). Then: *"Is such the fast that I choose, a day for a person to humble himself?"* (58:5). "Humble himself" is the humbling of the soul, the same words as their own complaint. What God does choose is turned outward: *"to let the oppressed go free"*, *"to share your bread with the hungry"*, *"not to hide yourself from your own flesh"* (58:6–7).

file_lines.section: What batch 1 adds to the account of choosing
file_lines.text: - **Refusing is choosing (Isa 7:15–16).** The act is one act with two sides, and refusing can go either way. The child refuses the evil. Ahaz refuses the sign, and the people refuse the gentle waters (8:6), with the same verb. This sharpens the test reading of Isa 65:12, which said that not answering and not listening are already choosing: in Isa 8:6 the refusal is named outright.

file_lines.section: Isaiah 56:4 — "who choose the things that please me and hold fast my covenant"
file_lines.text: Then he describes the eunuchs he means: *"who keep my Sabbaths, who choose the things that please me and hold fast my covenant"* (v4). The word "please" is H2654A, the same word as *"delight"* in Isaiah 65:12 and 66:4 (*"chose what I did not delight in"*, *"chose that in which I did not delight"*). Here the choosing goes the other way. These choose what the Lord delights in. The measure is the same as in those two oracles, the Lord's delight, and here it is met.

file_lines.section: Isaiah 56:4 — "who choose the things that please me and hold fast my covenant"
file_lines.text: - Choosing what the Lord delights in is the positive counterpart to choosing what he does not delight in (65:12, 66:4). The measure is the same.

file_lines.section: What batch 2 adds to the account of choosing
file_lines.text: - **Choosing what the Lord delights in (Isa 56:4).** This is the counterpart to Isaiah 65:12 and 66:4. With the three verses together, "the things that please me" and "what I did not delight in" are the two sides of one measure.

file_lines.text: ## Isaiah 65:12 — "chose what I did not delight in"

file_lines.section: Isaiah 65:12 — "chose what I did not delight in"
file_lines.text: The answer turns on their own word: *"I will destine you to the sword"* (v12). In Hebrew, "Destiny" (Meni, H4507) and "destine" (manah, H4487) come from the same root. They poured cups for Destiny, and the Lord destines them. What they chose to trust becomes the form their judgement takes.

file_lines.section: A note on the test
file_lines.text: - **"In whose eyes":** Jos 24:15 has *"evil in your eyes"*, and Isa 65:12 has *"evil in my eyes"*.

file_lines.section: Choosing in the human inner being — the account from the §2a readings

file_lines.section: Choosing has two sides
file_lines.text: Not answering is already choosing. *"when I called, you did not answer; when I spoke, you did not listen, but you did what was evil in my eyes and chose what I did not delight in"* (Isa 65:12; repeated in 66:4). The choosing of what the Lord does not delight in is where the not-listening ends up.

file_lines.section: Whose measure
file_lines.text: - **The Lord's eyes.** *"you did what was evil in my eyes"* (Isa 65:12). The measure is the Lord's sight.

file_lines.section: Whose measure
file_lines.text: - **The Lord's delight, failed.** *"chose what I did not delight in"* (Isa 65:12); *"chose that in which I did not delight"* (66:4).

file_lines.section: What follows the choice
file_lines.text: - They set *"cups of mixed wine for Destiny"*, and the Lord says *"I will destine you to the sword"*. "Destiny" and "destine" share a root (Isa 65:11–12).

file_lines.section: What changes the character
file_lines.text: - It gives way to *"evil in my eyes"*, the Lord's sight (Isa 65:12).

file_lines.section: What changes the character
file_lines.text: - **Delight (H2654A).** It is the soul's own delight in what it chose (Isa 66:3). It is the Lord's delight as the measure, either failed (Isa 65:12; 66:4) or met (Isa 56:4). *Why:* whose delight it is decides.

file_lines.text: ## Isaiah 66:3–4 — "These have chosen their own ways, and their soul delights in their abominations"

file_lines.section: Isaiah 66:3–4 — "These have chosen their own ways, and their soul delights in their abominations"
file_lines.text: Against that stands worship that looks right and is not: *"He who slaughters an ox is like one who kills a man; he who sacrifices a lamb, like one who breaks a dog’s neck"* … *"like one who blesses an idol"* (v3). The outward act is the same as before; what has gone wrong is inside. The verse says where: *"These have chosen their own ways, and their soul delights in their abominations."* Choosing and the soul’s delight stand side by side. They chose their own ways, and their soul (H5315) takes pleasure in what the Lord calls abominations.

file_lines.section: Isaiah 66:3–4 — "These have chosen their own ways, and their soul delights in their abominations"
file_lines.text: - their soul *"delights"* in abominations (v3)

file_lines.section: What batch 1 adds to the account of choosing
file_lines.text: - **Choosing goes with desire and delight.** It is paired with *"desired"* (1:29) and with the soul’s delight (66:3). In Isa 66 the delight word is the same on both sides, so the choice is a question of whose delight governs it.

file_lines.section: Isaiah 56:4 — "who choose the things that please me and hold fast my covenant"
file_lines.text: What follows in the chapter is the opposite. Israel's own watchmen *"are all without knowledge"*. They are *"shepherds who have no understanding; they have all turned to their own way, each to his own gain"* (v10–11). "Their own way" is the same phrase as in Isaiah 66:3, *"These have chosen their own ways"* (H1870G). The outsiders who choose what the Lord delights in are brought in. The insiders turn to their own way.

file_lines.section: What batch 3 adds to the account of choosing
file_lines.text: - **The pull before the choice.** *"Do not envy … and do not choose"* (Pro 3:31): the command reaches the envy as well as the choice. This stands beside batch 1, where *"desired"* is paired with *"chosen"* (Isa 1:29) and the soul's delight with choosing one's own ways (Isa 66:3).

file_lines.section: What draws it
file_lines.text: **Desire and delight.** Choosing comes paired with desire: *"the oaks that you desired … the gardens that you have chosen"* (Isa 1:29). It comes with the soul's delight: *"These have chosen their own ways, and their soul delights in their abominations"* (Isa 66:3).

file_lines.section: Whose measure
file_lines.text: - **The soul's own delight, set against the Lord's.** *"their soul delights in their abominations"* (Isa 66:3). The word is the same one again.

file_lines.section: What changes the character
file_lines.text: - **The choosing verb (H0977).** It is used for choosing a master (Jos 24:15), a place (Deu 23:16), a way (Psa 119:30; Isa 66:3), a preference (Pro 16:16), and a verdict (Job 34:4). *Why:* it is turned to whatever is set before a person.

file_lines.section: What changes the character
file_lines.text: - **Delight (H2654A).** It is the soul's own delight in what it chose (Isa 66:3). It is the Lord's delight as the measure, either failed (Isa 65:12; 66:4) or met (Isa 56:4). *Why:* whose delight it is decides.

file_lines.section: Isa 66:4
11. Isa 66:3 — chose their own ways; their soul delights in abominations
file_lines.text: - **Choice:** *"These have chosen their own ways, and their soul delights in their abominations"* (v3). The choosing and the soul's delight stand side by side. *"chose that in which I did not delight"* (v4).

file_lines.section: 11. Isa 66:3 — chose their own ways; their soul delights in abominations
file_lines.text: - **Outcome:** The Lord answers with a choice of his own: *"I also will choose harsh treatment for them and bring their fears upon them"* (v4). Their own fears are what comes on them. To those who tremble: *"it is they who shall be put to shame"* (v5).

file_lines.section: Isaiah 58:5: "Is such the fast that I choose, a day for a person to humble himself?"
file_lines.text: "Delight" in v2 (twice) is *ḥāpēṣ* (H2654A). It is the same word as *"chose that in which I did not delight"* in Isaiah 66:4, read in §2a. In v3 *"your own pleasure"* is the noun from the same root (H2656).

file_lines.section: Isaiah 58:5: "Is such the fast that I choose, a day for a person to humble himself?"
file_lines.text: - The self-humbling, done while seeking one's own pleasure and oppressing others, is not what he chooses (v3–5).

file_lines.section: Isaiah 66:3–4 — "These have chosen their own ways, and their soul delights in their abominations"
file_lines.text: The Lord’s answer is a choice of his own, in the same verb: *"I also will choose harsh treatment for them and bring their fears upon them"* (v4). What he brings is *their fears* (H4035): what they themselves dreaded. Set against v2 and v5, the contrast is in the inner being. The one who *"trembles at my word"* is looked on. Those who chose their own ways are given what they feared.

file_lines.section: Isaiah 66:3–4 — "These have chosen their own ways, and their soul delights in their abominations"
file_lines.text: The reason is given in the same words as 65:12: *"because when I called, no one answered, when I spoke, they did not listen; but they did what was evil in my eyes and chose that in which I did not delight"* (v4). Their choosing is the end of not answering and not listening.

file_lines.section: What batch 2 adds
file_lines.text: **Whose measure.** It comes up in four verses. Michal measures by *"the eyes of his servants' female servants"* (2Sa 6:20). The people in Jer 33:24 measure *"in their sight"*. Over against both, David celebrates *"before the Lord"* (2Sa 6:21), and Isa 49:7 gives the Lord's faithfulness and choosing. The same theme is in batch 1 (Deu 12:8) and in §2a ("whose measure").

file_lines.section: What batch 3 adds
file_lines.text: **Whose measure.** *"rejected by men but in the sight of God chosen"* (1Pe 2:4). This sits with batch 1 (Deu 12:8), batch 2 (2Sa 6:20; Jer 33:24) and §2a.

file_lines.section: Set against the chosen
file_lines.text: **A conclusion drawn from ruin.** *"'The Lord has rejected the two clans that he chose'? Thus they have despised my people so that they are no longer a nation in their sight"* (Jer 33:24). Others look at the state of the chosen, decide God has rejected them, and despise them on that ground. God's answer is that his choosing is as fixed as day and night (33:25–26).

file_lines.section: Set against the chosen
file_lines.text: **Whose eyes.** In four of these the measure is named, and it is set against God's: *"in his own eyes"* against the place God chooses (Deu 12:8); *"before the eyes of his servants' female servants"* against *"before the Lord"* (2Sa 6:20–21); *"in their sight"* (Jer 33:24); *"rejected by men but in the sight of God chosen"* (1Pe 2:4).

file_lines.section: What changes the character (#1919)
file_lines.text: - Others *"despised my people"*, concluding that God had rejected them (Jer 33:24; *nāʾaṣ*).

file_lines.section: M64 "choose": batch 3 — choosing of one's own accord, choosing together, and the wisdom sayings
2 Corinthians 8:17 — "being himself very earnest he is going to you of his own accord"
file_lines.text: The chapter is about giving to the poor saints. It opens with the Macedonians: *"in a severe test of affliction, their abundance of joy and their extreme poverty have overflowed in a wealth of generosity"* (v2). They gave *"according to their means … and beyond their means, of their own accord"* (v3). That is the same word as in v17 (G0830, *authairetos*, "self-chosen"). The order of their giving is set out: *"they gave themselves first to the Lord and then by the will of God to us"* (v5). Their own accord and the will of God stand side by side in one sentence.

file_lines.section: What batch 3 adds to the account of choosing
file_lines.text: - **Own accord alongside God's working.** Titus goes *"of his own accord"* after God *"put into the heart"* the care (2Cor 8:16–17). The Macedonians give *"of their own accord"*, having given themselves to the Lord *"by the will of God"* (8:3, 5). Both are named and neither cancels the other. This sits with batch 2 (the way to choose is taught) and the test (Psa 119:32, the heart enlarged by God).

file_lines.section: 3.10 One's own decision, desire, accord (8)
file_lines.text: - "they gave according to their means, as I can testify, and beyond their means, of their own accord" (2Cor 8:3)

file_lines.section: The words
file_lines.text: - **G0830, "of one's own accord".** One word, literally "self-chosen" (2Cor 8:3, 17).

file_lines.section: Own accord, and God at work
file_lines.text: The Macedonians gave *"of their own accord"*, and the order of their giving is set out: *"they gave themselves first to the Lord and then by the will of God to us"* (8:3, 5). The church's choice is joined to the Spirit's in the same verb: *"it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us"* (Act 15:28). The psalmist chooses, and asks God to give the room to carry it out: *"I will run in the way of your commandments when you enlarge my heart!"* (Psa 119:32). I read these verses as saying that what God puts into the heart becomes the person's own. The verses name both and do not explain how they fit.

file_lines.section: 2 Corinthians 8:17 — "being himself very earnest he is going to you of his own accord"

verses.text: But we ought always to give thanks to God for you, brothers beloved by the Lord, because God chose you as the firstfruits to be saved, through sanctification by the Spirit and belief in the truth.

observations.text: In 2Thess.2.13 'we ought always to give thanks to God for you' diverges from the meal-blessing sense dominant in the Gospels/Acts/1Cor occurrences of this cluster -- here thanksgiving is a sustained, obligatory disposition ('ought always') directed at other believers' salvation-status (election, sanctification, belief) rather than a single ritual act over food. The impact is to broaden eucharisteo from a punctual liturgical gesture to an ongoing pastoral duty of gratitude for others' spiritual condition.

In 2Thess.2.13, thanksgiving (G2168) co-occurs with M14 (brothers), M51 (beloved), M64 (chose), M16 (firstfruits), M79 (saved), M61 (sanctification), M13 (belief/truth, twice). Thanksgiving is the responsive frame surrounding this entire chain: it is offered specifically because of God's prior acts of choosing, sanctifying, and saving -- thanksgiving here functions as the grateful acknowledgment of the whole soteriological sequence rather than being caused by any single other M-code term alone.

In 2Thess.2.13, arche appears in the specialized sense 'firstfruits' rather than its more common gloss 'beginning/rule/authority' -- a divergence that carries covenantal-agricultural nuance (a consecrated, representative first portion) distinct from the term's dominant temporal or governmental senses elsewhere in the NT.
In 2Thess.2.13 'brothers' sits within the base NT sense of fellow believers; no notable divergence.
In 2Thess.2.13 'beloved by the Lord' sits within the base NT sense of God's settled love for believers; no notable divergence.
In 2Thess.2.13 'chose' sits within the base sense of God's electing choice; no notable divergence.
In 2Thess.2.13 'saved' sits within the base theological sense of eschatological salvation; no notable divergence.

In 2Thess.2.13 the sense shifts from a single concrete act (over food) to an ongoing obligation ('ought always to give thanks'), infinitive form, directed not at provision of a meal but at God's whole saving work (chosen, sanctified, saved) -- the nuance here is thanksgiving as continuous doxological duty rather than a discrete ritual moment, contrasting with the meal-occurrences.

Adding to the prior finding for 2Thess.2.13: from thanksgiving's own vantage, it functions specifically as an obligatory (opheilomen, 'we ought') response, distinguishing it from the other M-codes present (chosen M64, sanctification M61, belief/truth M13) which describe what God has done TO the believers, while thanksgiving alone names the believers' required responsive posture toward that whole complex.
In 2Thess.2.13 Paul and companions ('we', party) initiate the thanksgiving operation, directed toward God (party), on behalf of the Thessalonian brothers (party) for God's saving work toward them.

The large majority of G2168's occurrences (Rom.1.8; 1Cor.1.4; Eph.5.20; Col.1.3; 1Thess.5.18; Rev.11.17; 2Thess.2.13; Rom.16.4; 1Thess.2.13; 2Thess.1.3; 1Cor.1.14; 1Cor.14.18; Phil.1.3; 1Thess.1.2; Phlm.1.4; 1Cor.10.30; Col.1.12; 2Cor.1.11; Eph.1.16) share one core sense across the strong's own full occurrence list: an epistolary/liturgical, habitual first- or plural-person verb of thanking God, usually 'always'/'constantly' and grounded in some grace, faith, or benefit already received in the addressees or the speaker. This is the dominant register of the strong internally and forms the baseline against which the meal-blessing and single exceptional uses (below) stand out.

Thanksgiving is produced by prior reception of grace (M50, 1Cor.1.4), by observing another's faith or love (M13/M51, Rom.1.8, 2Thess.1.3), and by God's qualifying/electing/saving action (M64/M61/M79, Col.1.12, 2Thess.2.13) -- it is consistently downstream of these other characteristics/divine acts.
